🚀 Feature
Adopt a consistent convention of file extension for saved jit models.
Motivation
Technically the file can be named arbitrarily. But having and following a convention can help people know the format of the file.
Now the official tutorials are not consistent themselves. There are:

.pth: https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/jit.html#frequently-asked-questions
.zip: https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/Intro_to_TorchScript_tutorial.html#saving-and-loading-models
.pt: https://pytorch.org/tutorials/advanced/cpp_export.html#step-2-serializing-your-script-module-to-a-file

There are also use of .jit and .ts among users. Having a convention and use it consistently across tutorials would make the situation less confusing.
cc @gmagogsfm

🐛 Bug
Using a @torch.jit.script decorator on a somewhat simplified testcase results in a stack overflow during the second call of the decorated function. It is only reproducible using CUDA tensors. The first call of the function always succeeds.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Create a file called repr.py with the following contents:

import torch
from torch import Tensor


@torch.jit.script
def multilabel_confusion_matrix(y_true: Tensor, y_pred: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    true_and_pred = torch.mul(y_true, y_pred)
    tp_sum = torch.count_nonzero(true_and_pred, dim=0)
    pred_sum = torch.count_nonzero(y_pred, dim=0)
    true_sum = torch.count_nonzero(y_true, dim=0)

    fp = pred_sum - tp_sum
    fn = true_sum - tp_sum
    tp = tp_sum
    tn = y_true.shape[0] - tp - fp - fn

    return torch.stack([tn, fp, fn, tp])


y_true = torch.tensor(((1, 0), (0, 1))).cuda()
y_pred = torch.tensor(((1, 0), (0, 1))).cuda()
print(multilabel_confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).shape)
print(multilabel_confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).shape)

(optional) Run ulimit -s 128 to put a more reasonable cap on the depth of the call stack

The new torch.fft package is great, but it took me a while to figure out a data format change for going from torch.irfft to torch.fft.irfftn. torch.irfft expects complex inputs to be represented by 2 trailing dimensions, but torch.fft.irfftn expects torch.complex64 (or 128, etc) tensor.
Example:
# spectrum represents complex data with trailing dimension, as for old torch.irfft
# ie, spectrum.size() --> (N, C, D, H, W, 2) for my case

# Old
signal = torch.irfft(spectrum, 3, normalized=True, signal_sizes=(d, h, w))

# Silent bug
signal = torch.fft.irfftn(spectrum, s=(d, h, w), dim=(2, 3, 4), norm='ortho')

# Fixed
spectrum = torch.complex(spectrum[..., 0], spectrum[..., 1])
signal = torch.fft.irfftn(spectrum, s=(d, h, w), dim=(2, 3, 4), norm='ortho')
The old and new irfft implementations also don't seem to give exactly the same outputs all the time though. The difference hasn't affected me, but I'm curious where it comes from. Examples:
# Seems close:

torch.manual_seed(12345)
signal = torch.randn(1, 3, 10, 10, 10)
spectrum = torch.rfft(signal, 3, normalized=True)
recovered_old = torch.irfft(spectrum, 3, normalized=True, signal_sizes=(10, 10, 10))
recovered_new = torch.fft.irfftn(torch.complex(spectrum[..., 0], spectrum[..., 1]), dim=(2, 3, 4), s=(10, 10, 10), norm='ortho')

print(recovered_old - recovered_new).abs().max())
# >> Some small number, ~1e-6

# Not so close:
torch.manual_seed(12345)
spectrum = torch.randn(1, 3, 10, 10, 6, 2)    # Maybe this doesn't happen if spectrum is properly scaled?
recovered_old = torch.irfft(spectrum, 3, normalized=True, signal_sizes=(10, 10, 10))
recovered_new = torch.fft.irfftn(torch.complex(spectrum[..., 0], spectrum[..., 1]), dim=(2, 3, 4), s=(10, 10, 10), norm='ortho')

print(recovered_old - recovered_new).abs().max())
# >> Some not so small number, ~1.2
Finally, in order to reproduce old behavior closely norm='ortho' is the correct value for the new irfftn function. This can be figured out by referring to both functions' documentations, but it'd be nice to have described explicitly in the deprecation notices.

Since the old function torch.irfft is going to be deprecated in 1.8, it might help some other people to leave some related transitional notes in the documentation on these changes? I couldn't find any notes on this and it was causing errors in my work silently, so it took me some time to figure out what was happening.

The documentation for is_floating_point() reads:
Returns True if the data type of input is a floating point data type i.e., one of torch.float64, torch.float32 and torch.float16.

import torch
y = torch.tensor([[1.0]], dtype=torch.bfloat16)

The documentation for this method should be updated to include torch.bfloat16.

The task
The task is to pick an operator on the list (or a group of them) and implement batching rules for them. I will add github handles next to the operators that are currently being worked on and mark completed ones as done.
How to reproduce
Pick an operator from the above list (e.g., Tensor.fill_). Attempt to run it inside a vmap:
>>> import torch
>>> from torch import vmap
>>> x = torch.randn(64, 3)
>>> result = vmap(lambda x: x.fill_(1))(x)
/scratch/rzou/pt/whiteboard-env/bin/ipython:4: UserWarning: Batching rule not implemented for aten::fill_.Scalar falling back to slow (for loop) implementation (Triggered internally
at  ../aten/src/ATen/BatchedFallback.cpp:68.)

It should raise a warning that the batching rule has not been implemented.
Context
vmap is a higher-order vectorization operator. It takes in a function f and returns a new function that maps the f over some dimension of the inputs. The new function has similar semantics to performing a for-loop over the mapped dimension:
inputs = torch.randn(N, 3)
f = lambda x: x.clamp(min=0)
expected = torch.stack([f(inputs[i]) for i in range(N)])
result = torch.vmap(f)(inputs)
assert torch.allclose(result, expected)
Instead of performing a for-loop to compute expected, the user could have vectorized their computation by straight up calling clamp: expected2 = inputs.clamp(min=0). However, for more complicated functions, like F.conv2d, vectorizing is not as obvious. In some cases, like efficient Jacobian/Hessian computation, vectorization isn't possible by the user because they cannot control what happens inside of the autograd engine. One of the targeted use cases for vmap is to speed up batched gradient computation in PyTorch.
How vmap works is that a "batching rule" is defined for each operator. The batching rule defines how to perform the operation on inputs with extra dimensions (that we refer to as the "batch dimensions").

Issue description
We use OrderedDict a lot in Pytorch and Torchvision. Since the native dict already supports the insert order after python 3.7 (Reference), shall we move to the native dict in pytorch implementations? Or at least for user interfaces (such as nn.Sequential, state_dict and load_state_dict), so that we can get it more convenient.
nn.Sequential Example
Python dict Docs
Python OrderedDict Docs
Previous code
torch.nn.Sequential(OrderedDict([('id', torch.nn.Identity()), ('id2', torch.nn.Identity())]))
Expectation
torch.nn.Sequential({'id': torch.nn.Identity(), 'id2': torch.nn.Identity()})
Currently, this usage will raise TypeError: dict is not a Module subclass
cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser

Today in test_ops.py we have a single test for out= behavior:

  
    
      pytorch/test/test_ops.py
    
    
         Line 306
      in

           def test_out(self, device, dtype, op): 
        
    
  


This test

only works if the operator has a single tensor output
only asserts that the out= variant works when passing an empty_like of the output

This is a good start, but we can do better.
Conceptually, operators that support out= should work as follows (see also #41027 (comment) for additional background):

the operator's computation is independent of the out= argument
the result of the computation is "safe" copied to the out= argument

"Safe" copying is like regular copying except it requires that:

the tensors are on the same device (Note: not just same device type, same device)
when the operation has a "computation type", then the "dtype kind" of the copied to tensor is at least the "dtype kind" of the copied from tensor; PyTorch has four "dtype kinds": boolean, integer, float, and complex. So we do not permit computing in complex and copying to float, for example, or computing in an integer type and copying to bool.

There is one caveat to this behavior: if the out= tensor has zero elements then it may be resized before the copy. See:

  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/Resize.h
    
    
         Line 17
      in
      6d6e9ab
    
  
  
    

        
          
           CAFFE2_API void resize_output(Tensor& output, IntArrayRef shape); 
        
    
  


If the out= tensor is resized then the operation may also edit its strides. The device or dtype of the out= tensor may never change, however.
To test out= better, then, PyTorch needs to add multiple tests that do the following:
(updated to reflect #53259)

work with operators that produce any number of tensor outputs

this can probably be detected programmatically and the metadata supports_tensor_out removed


pass tensors full of NaNs as out tensors to verify the out= tensors are not read and are completely written to
pass tensors with no elements, tensors of the correct size, discontiguous tensors of the correct size, and tensors of the incorrect size to out to validate the resizing logic

tensors with no elements should be resized, tensors of the correct size should be used, and tensors of the incorrect size should throw a warning
verify that functions validate out's dtype and device properly


verify the computation with out= is equivalent to the computation without it + copying to the out= tensor
pass the input tensor to out= and verify either that the input tensor is correctly modified in place or that a runtime error is thrown
verify that functions enforce "safe" dtype casting (as described above)
validate that inplace operations are equivalent to using the inplace argument as the out parameter

To avoid overburdening the CI machinery, these tests should probably continue to run on only the first sample input and not every sample input. However, we should also verify that each operator's "first" sample input is a nontrivial and nondegenerate input, and document with a comment that this should be the case. 📚 Documentation
In the docs for torch.argmax and torch.argmin there is a note that states: If there are multiple minimal values then the indices of the first minimal value are returned.
First of all, for torch.argmax the note should say "maximum" values, not "minimal".
Second, both torch.argmax and torch.argmin return the index of the last value, not the first, e.g.:
>>> x = torch.FloatTensor([0,0,0,0,0])
>>> torch.argmax(x)
tensor(4)
>>> torch.argmin(x)
tensor(4)

So, either the note is incorrect or the functions are incorrect.
Other related issues such as this one say that the results are not deterministic, but they are. There's also an issue regarding numpy pairity (although argmax and argmin are not mentioned in the issue), however numpy returns the first minimal/maximum value, which mirrors the PyTorch documentation but not the actual result of the argmax/argmin functions.

🐛 Bug
To me, it seems like the interplay between requiring gradients and the profiling executor/fuser fallback seems not ideal:

in the fuser1 (TensorExpr) and fuser2 (CudaFuser), if I run a few grad-requiring tensors through my model and then run non-grad-requiring, it will run into the DifferentiableSubgraph and give me a grad-requiring output even though none of the inputs requires gradient. (It will also run a kernel outputting intermediates that we don't need, so perf loss...)
in the fuser2 (CudaFuser) the CudaFusionGuard doesn't check for requires grad, so if I run a few non-grad-requiring tensors first, and feed a grad-requiring input, it'll drop the gradient (this is different for fuser1 where the typecheck checks for requires grad and then drops into the fallback).

To me it would seem that if we want to pull off the fallback stuff, we would properly guard DifferentiableGraph with what requires grad and the fusion guards with nothing requires grad (we might also have cases where which gradients are required varies).
To Reproduce
for fuser in ["fuser1", "fuser2"]:
    for rq in [True, False]:
        c = torch.jit.fuser(fuser)
        c.__enter__()

        def ratio_iou(x1, y1, w1, h1, x2, y2, w2, h2):
            xi = torch.max(x1, x2)                                  # Intersection left
            yi = torch.max(y1, y2)                                  # Intersection top
            wi = torch.clamp(torch.min(x1+w1, x2+w2) - xi, min=0.)  # Intersection width
            hi = torch.clamp(torch.min(y1+h1, y2+h2) - yi, min=0.)  # Intersection height
            area_i = wi * hi                                        # Area Intersection
            area_u = w1 * h1 + w2 * h2 - wi * hi                    # Area Union
            return area_i / torch.clamp(area_u, min=1e-5)           # Intersection over Union

        ratio_iou_scripted = torch.jit.script(ratio_iou)

        x1, y1, w1, h1, x2, y2, w2, h2 = torch.randn(8, 100, 1000, device='cuda', requires_grad=not rq).exp()

        for i in range(10):
            ratio_iou_scripted.graph_for(x1, y1, w1, h1, x2, y2, w2, h2)
        #print(ratio_iou_scripted.graph_for(x1, y1, w1, h1, x2, y2, w2, h2))

        x1, y1, w1, h1, x2, y2, w2, h2 = torch.randn(8, 100, 1000, device='cuda', requires_grad=rq).exp()
        print(fuser, x1.requires_grad, ratio_iou_scripted(x1, y1, w1, h1, x2, y2, w2, h2).requires_grad)
Expected behavior
requires_grad of output same as for input.

PyTorch master.

This used to be handled by the ArgSpec mechanism.

🐛 Bug
detach_() does not perform in-place detachment from the computation graph for a node that already has children. If a gradient computation is issued after the detachment, gradients are still propagated through the node.
To Reproduce
import torch

a = torch.zeros((2, 2), requires_grad=True)
b = 2 * a
c = b.sum()
b.detach_()
c.backward()
print(a.grad)

Expected behavior
Gradients should not be propagated through the detached node, and the past parents should not be referenced anymore, making them collectable by the garbage collector if no further references exist to them.
With the current behavior, it is not possible to perform truncated BPTT with a fixed truncation length without performing redundant computations:

This is especially important in cases where the loss at time t also depends on the model output at time t + c. The sensible thing in such a case would be to have a computation graph at least "c timesteps long". This would be possible if in-place detachment worked as stated above, by detaching the model output at timestep t - c and calling loss.backward(retain_graph=True). nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
Either:

A way to go from a stateful NN Module to a functional (read: functions only and stateless) NN Module.
An alternative, functional NN Module API in addition to our current NN API.

Motivation
It is difficult to use the torch.autograd.functional APIs with NN modules because these APIs require the user to pass the parameters to a function. For example, consider the torch.autograd.functional.jacobian API:
torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(func, inputs, create_graph=False, strict=False)
An nn.Module holds some parameters, but we would like to grab those parameters and send it through the jacobian function. It is not sufficient to do:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.autograd.functional as F
from functools import partial

N = 2
model = nn.Linear(3, 5)
data = torch.randn(N, 3)
params = tuple(model.parameters())
func = lambda *params: model(data)
jacs = F.jacobian(func, params)
This returns jacobians that are full of zeros, which is not what we wanted. The higher level autograd API takes the Tensors to differentiate (params in this case) and preprocesses them to create new Tensors that record autograd history. The reason why this returns zero jacobians is because the params being passed to func don't actually get used.
As a quick "proof-by-example" that the jacobians shouldn't be zero, the following gives non-zero jacobians:
def run_model(weight, bias, data):
    return nn.functional.linear(data, weight, bias)

F.jacobian(partial(run_model, data=data), params)
Furthermore, it is difficult to use the prototype torch.vmap API on an nn.Module for the same reason: there is currently no PyTorch-blessed mechanism to, given an nn.Module, create a stateless callable that does the same thing as the module.
Pitch
Here's one possibility for the API that implements a way to go from a stateful nn.Module to a functional variant of it. The building blocks for this is already implemented in our functional autograd benchmarks and higher has something similar:
def make_functional(model: nn.Module) -> "params", Callable[Tuple["data", "params"], Any]:
    """Given an nn.Module, returns its Parameters
    and a Callable that takes in inputs to the module and the params and returns the output.
    """
    pass
Here's how one would call it with functional.jacobian:
# pseudocode
model: nn.Module = ...
data: Tensor = ...
params, func = make_functional(model)
F.jacobian(partial(func, data), params)  # Compute jacobian w.r.t to module parameters
F.jacobian(partial(func, params=params), data)  # Compute jacobian w.r.t to module inputs
We've omitted some details of how this API should work:

how should "Params" look like? How does the user create a different set of Params or operate over them?
What about buffers that are registered on modules? Do we pull them out as well?
How does this work with modules that mutate internal state, like nn.BatchNorm?

deepmind/dm-haiku has some interesting ideas for the above two questions that we can look to for inspiration.
Alternatives
I'm not sure that we can actually remove state from all of our nn.Modules. We can certainly do this for most of them, though.
One alternative to a NN Module functional API is to tell PyTorch users to always use the nn.functional variant of a module if they wish to use the autograd.functional APIs (e.g., use F.conv2d instead of nn.Conv2d). However, users use the NN API because it is handy: carrying around all of the parameters manually sometimes unwieldy, especially if you built a model out of some number of nested layers and have a large number of parameters to keep track of
A stretch goal that may be out of scope for this is "An alternative, functional NN Module API in addition to our current NN API". We may want something like this if we're planning on having a way to make our NN modules more functional anyways. There have been a number of NN module designs in JAX that work with a functional API. One example is stax, which models Modules as an (init_fn, apply_fn) pair. If you have JAX installed, here's how one gets the jacobian of a Linear layer with stax:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax.experimental.stax as stax
from functools import partial

key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
N = 2
data = jnp.ones([N, 3], dtype=jnp.float32)
init_fn, apply_fn = stax.Dense(5)

_, params = init_fn(key, data.shape)
# jax.jacrev is the API to compute the jacobian using reverse-mode AD
jax.jacrev(partial(apply_fn, inputs=data))(params)
Here's a similar example, but using the deepmind/dm-haiku library. haiku.transform turns what looks like a stateful Module (it's not actually stateful) into an (init_fn, apply_fn) pair.
import haiku as hk
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from functools import partial

key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
data = jnp.ones([2, 3])

def model(data):
    mlp = hk.Linear(5)
    return mlp(data)

func = hk.transform(model)
params = func.init(key, data)
jax.jacrev(lambda params: func.apply(params, key, data))(params)
Additional context
facebookresearch/higher does something similar: https://github.com/facebookresearch/higher
JAX, a very functional framework, has a few different NN libraries that are all functional all with some interesting design choices.
